title: Evaluating LLMs as a Bridge Between Cyber Threats and Business Risk

ai_profile.summary: This paper evaluates locally deployable open-weight large language models to bridge the gap between technical cyber threat intelligence and executive decision-making. The study tests five prompt strategies against real-world incident reports using a structured rubric scored by both an AI instrument and human analysts. Results indicate that prompt architecture is the primary driver of output quality, while AI-only scoring often overestimates accuracy, necessitating human review. This study evaluates whether locally hosted large language models can effectively convert technical cyber threat intelligence into executive-ready business risk summaries. Using a controlled experimental design, the research tests Gemma3:27b under various prompt strategies to determine its reliability in generating consistent outputs without cloud infrastructure. The findings emphasize that while local deployment offers security benefits and accessibility for small teams, human analyst review remains essential for quality control. This research evaluates Large Language Models (LLMs) to determine if they can reduce the drafting burden on analysts while clarifying that AI cannot replace analyst judgment in assessing organizational relevance or escalation thresholds. The study uses a corpus of 20 cyber incident reports from public security vendors, generating 1,000 AI executive summaries across five distinct prompt strategies ranging from minimal instruction to maximum structure. A significant design challenge arose with Strategy S3, where the original plan to use a fully written one-shot example report caused the model to reproduce content from that example rather than processing the source reports due to retrieval pipeline limitations. This study evaluates large language models for translating cyber threat intelligence into executive-ready summaries using a four-dimension weighted rubric. While the aggregate performance of 1,000 AI-generated reports fell below the passing threshold, specific prompt strategies like S4 significantly improved pass rates to 73.5%. However, human-analyst inter-rater exercises revealed that the AI scoring instrument overestimated quality in many cases. The study evaluates Large Language Models (LLMs) by testing their ability to generate cybersecurity intelligence reports under varying constraints, ranging from minimal formatting to explicit structural templates. Results indicate that while specific requirements like the BLUF principle significantly improved report structure, they failed to compensate for deficiencies in actionability and analytical rigor within the scoring rubric. Additionally, the model exhibited a tendency to hallucinate definitions for technical acronyms when attempting to expand them, a behavior mitigated only by providing correct context or avoiding expansion entirely. The study evaluates Large Language Models as a bridge between cyber threats and business risk, analyzing how prompt design affects report quality across four threat categories. While the model performs well on technical reports like ransomware and zero-day exploits, it struggles significantly with supply chain attacks due to their complex causal chains. Furthermore, human analysts and an AI instrument showed substantial disagreement in scoring reports, indicating that individual assessments can vary greatly between rating systems. The study evaluates Large Language Models (LLMs) as a bridge between cyber threat intelligence (CTI) and business risk assessment, finding that AI-generated reports are significantly faster to produce than human-authored ones. While the AI instrument scores reports at a 73.5% pass rate, human analysts consistently diverged from these scores, revealing a 61.7% verdict-flip rate and suggesting actual quality is lower under expert judgment. The research concludes that prompt architecture is the primary determinant of output quality rather than model capability alone. This study evaluates a locally deployed Gemma3:27b model as a bridge between cyber threat intelligence and business decision-making using a four-dimensional scoring rubric. While AI-generated reports show lower pass rates compared to other categories, the research concludes that prompt engineering can produce passing-quality executive reports on consumer-grade hardware without enterprise infrastructure. Future work must address model drift, replicate findings across different model families, and test multi-document synthesis capabilities. The study reveals that AI scoring instruments systematically overestimate the quality of cyber threat intelligence reports compared to human expert judgment, with significant divergence in pass rates and verdicts. While AI models often reproduce exemplar content rather than analyzing source documents due to semantic retrieval constraints, combining accessible AI tools with rigorous evaluation disciplines can transform these capabilities into reliable workflows. The research provides a reproducible framework for practitioners to adapt scoring rubrics and build empirical records in the field of cyber threat intelligence. The provided text outlines a framework for rewriting cyber threat intelligence reports into executive-level summaries using the BLUF methodology. It defines specific roles, such as a senior analyst at a financial institution, and establishes strict constraints to ensure clarity for non-technical decision-makers. The document emphasizes connecting technical threats directly to business consequences like operational disruption or reputational damage without including raw data. This document outlines a framework for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) to bridge cyber threats and business risk, authored by Arcadio Aguilar for senior executives. It provides strict guidelines for translating technical threat intelligence into clear business impacts, focusing on operational disruption and financial consequences rather than system details. The text emphasizes using the Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF) methodology to ensure executive reports deliver immediate, decisive conclusions before supporting context. The document presents a comparative analysis of AI scoring versus human analyst evaluation for cybersecurity threat reports, highlighting significant performance gaps and inter-rater discrepancies. It details how different prompt strategies (Baseline, Template, BLUF, One-Shot) impact pass rates across various threat categories like ransomware and supply chain attacks. Furthermore, the study quantifies the time savings achieved by using AI tools, noting that while AI generation is rapid, human analysts still require substantially more time per report.
